hints: Focus on what NaOH(aq) under reflux does to a halogenoalkane, it swaps the halogen for OH without changing the carbon skeleton.
Since the alcohol made is pentan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, X must be 2-halopentane with the halogen on carbon 2.
Now apply the same substitution idea with $\text{CN}^-$ in place of $\text{OH}^-$, the CN simply takes the exact position where the halogen was.
walkthrough:
**Work backwards from the alcohol**

Think like a detective. Aqueous NaOH under reflux converts a halogenoalkane to an alcohol by nucleophilic substitution.

$$\text{R-X + OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-OH + X}^-$$

**Identify X**

The product is pentan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The OH is on carbon 2, so the halogen in X must also have been on carbon 2.

$$\text{X = CH}_3\text{CH(Hal)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \text{ (2-halopentane)}$$

**Swap halogen for cyanide**

Heating with KCN in ethanol does the same type of substitution, but $\text{CN}^-$ is the nucleophile instead of $\text{OH}^-$.

$$\text{R-X + CN}^- \rightarrow \text{R-CN + X}^-$$

**Draw the nitrile product**

Put CN on carbon 2 of the pentane chain. You get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is 2-methyl substituted at the second carbon, exactly the branched structure shown in the correct option.

options.A: This is pentanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, a straight chain nitrile. It would come from 1-halopentane, which would have given pentan-1-ol with NaOH(aq), not pentan-2-ol.
options.B: This is 2-cyanobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CN)CH}_3$, which has only 5 carbons in total including the CN carbon. Our starting material has 5 carbons plus the new CN carbon, so this is one carbon too short.
options.C: This is hexanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, a straight chain with CN at the end. This confuses substitution with addition to a carbonyl. KCN here substitutes the halogen in place, it does not add an extra carbon to the end of the chain.
options.D: This is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, with CN on carbon 2. It is exactly what you get when 2-halopentane undergoes nucleophilic substitution by $\text{CN}^-$, matching the position of the OH in pentan-2-ol.
